lines: Last chapter's tree was already optimal, by its own measure. Every search cost the smallest number of comparisons a tree possibly could.
But a comparison and a trip to disk stopped being the same thing a long time ago. This chapter is about what you pay for the second one.
Here's the one new constraint: every leaf sits at the exact same depth, and nothing short of the root is ever less than half full.
That second rule is doing more work than it looks like. It's the whole reason this tree's height stays predictable at all.
This leaf just took in one key too many.
Before the reveal, think about what a structure with a hard capacity limit is actually forced to do once that limit is crossed.
answer: It splits into two leaves, and one key moves up to the parent to keep routing correct.
Nothing about the keys already in that leaf changes. The split only decides which half each one now belongs to.

lines: Watch what each half gets handed. The leaf copies its middle key upward, because that key still has to live somewhere a search can find it.
An inner node does the opposite: it pushes that key up and keeps no copy at all, because an inner node was never storing anything but a route.
If the split climbs all the way to the root, the tree gains a brand new top level. That's the only way this structure ever grows taller.
Now the opposite failure: a delete just left a leaf under its floor.
Guess at the fix before it's shown. A structure with a floor, not just a ceiling, has exactly two honest ways to recover from going under it.
answer: Take one key from a sibling that can spare it, or, if none can, combine with one entirely.
Borrowing changes two neighbors' key counts and nothing else. A combine is the heavier move, and it's the last resort, not the first.

lines: A borrow is cheap on purpose: one key slides across a boundary, and the tree's shape never moves.
Merging is the expensive branch, chosen only when borrowing has nowhere to come from, and it's the single operation in this whole topic that can make the tree shorter.
A range query doesn't want one key. It wants everything between two of them, in order.
Once the first matching leaf is found, every leaf after it is reached by a direct link to its neighbor, not by climbing back up and coming down again.
Fanout is just arithmetic: however many keys and pointers physically fit in one page, that's how many children a node can route to.
Height falls out of that arithmetic too. Grow the fanout, and the same number of keys needs dramatically fewer levels to reach.
Put the identical set of keys through both trees and the gap isn't subtle.
One pays for a trip to disk at every single comparison. The other reads an entire page's worth of comparisons in one trip, and a realistic page shrinks that gap even further.
Nothing in this topic was taken on faith, so here's what actually got measured.
Splitting and modifying a real tree, scanning across its linked leaves instead of climbing back to the top for every match, and the fanout-and-height formula checked directly against a billion keys.
